title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:2–4)
hookLine: the nations will beat swords into ploughshares and learn war no more

lines: A STATUE AT THE UNITED NATIONS.
cards: In the garden of the United Nations in New York stands a bronze statue of a muscular man. He holds a hammer high over his head.

In his other hand is a sword, and he's bending its blade; the end is already curling into the shape of a plow. The statue was a gift from the Soviet Union, during the Cold War, while both sides were building bombs.
Its title comes from an old Hebrew prophet, writing in a small kingdom squeezed between empires.

teach.h: ALL NATIONS STREAMING TO THE MOUNTAIN.
teach.b: Isaiah, chapter two, sees a day to come: the mountain of the Lord's house raised above the hills, and all nations streaming to it. Not dragged.
Streaming, like a river running uphill, saying, let's go up, so he'll teach us his ways.

Then, in the King James Bible: "and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more."
A plowshare is the iron blade that cuts the soil; a pruning hook trims vines. Iron was precious, so you didn't bury or hide it. You reforged it.
The same metal that killed now feeds. And the last phrase: they shall not learn war any more.

teach.h: WAR IS LEARNED, SO IT CAN BE UNLEARNED.
teach.b: War is something learned, so it can be unlearned. The same vision appears almost word for word in the prophet Micah, who adds that everyone will sit under their own vine and fig tree, with no one to make them afraid.
The prophet Joel turns the image around, calling people to beat their plowshares into swords for battle. The Bible knows both directions; Isaiah's points to the end of the story.

Christians often read it as a promise of God's kingdom, and hear Jesus' blessing on the peacemakers as a call to live toward it now. Some, Mennonites and Quakers among them, take it as a call to refuse war entirely.
Others hold it as the goal while believing defense can be just.

teach.h: NEITHER SHALL THEY LEARN WAR ANY MORE.
teach.b: And an old African American spiritual, Down by the Riverside, carries the last phrase into song: study war no more.

how: Isaiah 2:4 is often read in Advent and at services of prayer for peace; the phrase study war no more comes from the African American spiritual Down by the Riverside, sung in churches and at peace gatherings.

o: a vine-trimming tool, reforged from a spear
a farmer's hook for hanging up grain sacks
a curved blade soldiers used in close battle

games.q: what's inside the vision — tap the pairs.
p: everyone under their own vine and fig tree

s: the vision says weapons will be buried and forgotten
they're reforged: the same iron becomes tools for farming.
the same vision appears almost word for word in Micah
Micah 4:3, adding that everyone will sit under their own vine and fig tree.
the Bible only ever turns swords into plows
Joel 3:10 turns plowshares into swords. Isaiah's direction points to the end of the story.

games.q: you're a farmer in Isaiah's vision, holding a sword you no longer need. iron is precious. what do you do with it?
o: hang it on the wall as a trophy.
games.why: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares." the same metal that killed is reforged to feed, and war is no longer learned.

practice: Think of one small weapon you carry, a sharp tone, a grudge you sharpen, a habit of winning arguments, a post you keep meaning to write, and hold it in your mind like a piece of iron.
Picture the hammer, and the blade slowly becoming a tool: a conversation instead of a jab, help instead of a grudge. If you pray, you can pray for peace in one place you know of, by name.

wordCard.voice: Pruninghook. The vine-trimming tool Isaiah pictures a spear reforged into, iron that once killed now feeding people, and war itself unlearned.

orig.note: Hebrew: and they shall not learn war any more. war is something learned.

carryVoice: Your line: study war no more. What was learned can be unlearned. That's day four hundred sixty-four.
